--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.degrees()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: Get degree for all nodes in the graph. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.degrees()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: Get degree for all nodes in the graph. title: >- [Graph.degrees()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Get degree for all nodes in the graph. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Get degree for all nodes in the graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L43251-L43365){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.degrees( attr_name=None, return_dict=False, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Degree of every node](../assets/graphs/degrees.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A seven-node graph, a strip of three triangles A to E with a tail F, G, each node shaded by its degree. Hub C has the most neighbors and the darkest shading, and the table lists C 4, then B, D, E 3, A, F 2, and G 1." width="100%"} For directed graphs, returns total degree (in-degree + out-degree). For undirected graphs, returns the number of neighbors. This batch method computes `get_degree()` for every node in one call and automatically stores results in the node DataFrame. Degree is the simplest measure of how connected a node is. It is useful for: - spotting hubs and poorly connected nodes at a glance - storing degree as a node attribute so it can drive later steps, such as sizing or coloring nodes in a plot or filtering with `select_nodes()` - a quick baseline before reaching for more expensive centrality measures More precisely, a node's degree here is its number of incident edges: parallel edges each count, and in undirected graphs a self-loop counts twice. Edge weights are ignored (each edge counts as `1`). For in- or out-degree alone, use `get_in_degree()` or `get_out_degree()`. With `return_dict=False` the degrees are written to the node DataFrame; with `return_dict=True` they are only returned. Note that `get_node_df()` always ends with a live `degree` column, so with the default `attr_name=` the stored attribute appears under that same column name; pick another `attr_name=` if you want a separate snapshot column. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Column name to store degree values in the node DataFrame. If `None` (default), automatically uses `degree`. Overwrites column if it already exists. [return_dict]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, returns a dictionary mapping node IDs to degrees without writing anything to the graph. If `False` (default), stores in NDF and returns self for chaining. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Union[dict[int, int], Graph]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_dict=` is `True`: dictionary mapping node IDs to degree values. If `return_dict=` is `False` (default): returns self for method chaining. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} `A` is connected to both other nodes and has degree `2`, while `B` and `C` each have degree `1`. The values are stored on the nodes and shown in the node DataFrame: ::: {#ec4c9a30 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("A", "C")]) .degrees(return_dict=False) ) graph.get_node_df().select(["id", "degree"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: In a directed graph, in- and out-edges are added together. Every node in this three-node graph has degree `2`, even though `A` only sends edges and `C` only receives them: ::: {#ff98c152 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} directed = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("A", "C"), ("B", "C")]) ) degs = directed.degrees(return_dict=True) {directed.get_label_from_id(nid): d for nid, d in sorted(degs.items())} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {'A': 2, 'B': 2, 'C': 2} ``` ::: ::: Because it stores results as a node attribute, `degrees()` chains directly into other attribute-driven methods like `rescale_node_attrs()` -- handy for sizing nodes by degree in a visualization: ::: {#dbd794ea .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.karate_club() .degrees(return_dict=False) .rescale_node_attrs( node_attr_from="degree", node_attr_to="size", range=[0.5, 2.0], ) ) graph.describe() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Name of Graph : Zachary's Karate Club Number of nodes : 34 Number of edges : 78 Directed : False Density : 0.14 Average degree (min, max) : 4.59 (1, 17) Connected : True Number of connected components : 1 Tree : False Bipartite : False Computations: - degrees() -> attr: 'degree' (34 of 34 nodes) Node aesthetics: - size <- degree via rescale (range: [0.5, 2.0]) (11 unique values, 34 of 34 nodes) ``` ::: :::
